summary: Registrations in the IANA "RTP Payload Format Media Types" registry were often skipped, even though RFC 8088 recommended them. To simplify things, this RFC closes that special registry and relies only on the general "Media Types" registry for RTP payload formats.

plainLanguage.summary: There were two lists tracking the same things and people kept forgetting one. This closes the extra list so there is only one place to look.

questions: why was the rtp payload format media types registry closed
where to register rtp payload media types
what is the purpose of the media types registry
how do you define a new rtp payload format
subtitle: Consolidating where RTP payload format media types are registered.

tldr.problem: When authors defined new RTP payload formats, they sometimes forgot to register them in the IANA "RTP Payload Format Media Types" registry, creating inconsistency and redundancy since they also had to register in the general "Media Types" registry.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC closes the specialized RTP registry and updates RFC 8088 to require registration only in the general "Media Types" registry, making the process simpler and eliminating duplication.
tldr.outcome: There is now one authoritative place to find and register RTP payload formats, making compliance easier and the registration process clearer.

facts.label: Closes
facts.value: IANA "RTP Payload Format Media Types" registry

today: RFC 9751 is a Standards Track document published in March 2025. The "RTP Payload Format Media Types" registry is now closed. All new RTP payload formats must be registered in the IANA "Media Types" registry only, and RFC 8088 has been updated to reflect this change.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RTP payload formats define how different types of content (audio, video, application data) are encoded and transmitted using the Real-time Transport Protocol. When authors created new payload formats, they were recommended to register them in two places: the general IANA "Media Types" registry and a specialized "RTP Payload Format Media Types" registry.

In practice, authors often skipped the specialized registry. This created an incomplete registry that served no real purpose, since the general Media Types registry already tracked everything needed for signaling and avoiding collisions. The specialized registry was rarely consulted and had no documented purpose beyond duplicating information already recorded elsewhere.
sections.plainLanguage: RTP payload formats are recipes for how to send audio, video, or other data over the internet. They needed to be registered in two places, but people kept forgetting one because they were tracking the same thing.

sections.title: Why Close the Registry
sections.content:
The "RTP Payload Format Media Types" registry existed but its origin was unclear. Looking back at RFC 4855, which supposedly described its maintenance, yielded no actual instructions or rules. Further investigation found no specification that had formally established the registry.

Since the registry served only to track which media types had RTP formats—information available through other means and already required in the Media Types registry—closing it eliminated redundancy without loss. All RTP payload formats must already be registered in the Media Types registry for use in signaling protocols and session descriptions.
sections.plainLanguage: The old registry had no clear rules and nobody really needed it. Everything important is already in the main list.

sections.title: Origins and Evolution
sections.content:
The registry's creation was never formally documented. Attempts to trace its establishment yielded no RFC text or official record. RFC 4855 is cited as providing maintenance instructions, but review found no such guidance in that document. It appears the registry may have been created through email discussion or an Area Director request, but this context has been lost.

This lack of formal documentation contributed to the registry's neglect. Without clear rules or a documented purpose, maintainers and authors had no reference to consult, making the registry seem optional and leading to incomplete registrations.
sections.plainLanguage: Nobody could find where the old list came from or what the rules were supposed to be. It was probably started informally and then forgotten.

sections.title: Update to RFC 8088
sections.content:
RFC 8088 "How to Write an RTP Payload Format" had instructed authors that when registering a media type, they must also request registration in the "RTP Payload Format Media Types" registry. This RFC updates that instruction.

The new text removes the requirement for the specialized registry. Instead, it simply says: when registering a media type for an RTP payload format, request that IANA register it in the "Media Types" registry. This is the only registration step needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The old instruction said to register in two places. The new one says just register in one place—the main list.

sections.title: IANA Actions
sections.content:
This RFC directed IANA to perform three actions. First, it populated the "RTP Payload Format Media Types" registry with known RTP payload formats at the time of publication, capturing formats that had been registered or implemented. This included formats like Opus audio, VP8 video, EVRC audio variants, and several others across audio, video, application, and text subtypes.

Second, it formally closed the registry to future registrations and added a note explaining that the registry is now closed and redundant with the Media Types registry. Third, it corrected the registry's note to document that RFC 4855 does not actually define how the registry should work, clarifying the historical confusion about the registry's origins.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA added all the known formats that were already being used, then locked the old list so nobody could add to it anymore.

references.text: Westerlund, M., "How to Write an RTP Payload Format", RFC 8088, May 2017.
